title: Inference Reliability Pitch for Platform Teams
content:
Purpose
This one-page play is an engineering-oriented positioning brief targeted squarely at platform teams and internal infra buyers. It explains why Redwood is the pragmatic choice when the ask is: predictable SLAs, clear unit economics, and low operational drag for LLM inference across hosted, reserved, and private footprints.

Core thesis (single-line)
Platform teams buy inference infrastructure to make LLM features reliably cheap, debuggable, and rollout-safe — Redwood is the only vendor that treats serving as a first-class infrastructure problem (not an API bolt-on).

Problem statements we lead with
- Unpredictable unit economics: token bills spike when traffic patterns change or cold-starts dominate.
- Latency outliers break UX: a few long-polling requests ruin session quality and user experience metrics.
- Operational cognitive load: building batching, KV cache, quantization, and rollout tooling in-house slows feature velocity.
- Compliance/segmentation complexity: teams need the same runtime in-hosted mode and in a VPC/on-prem for regulated product lines.

Key Redwood value pillars (short bullets for deck copy)
- Deterministic economics: batching, prefix/KV caching, and workload-aware routing that materially reduces per-token cost without manual tuning.
- SLA-grade latency: architecture and fallbacks built for p50/p95 SLOs; automatic model variant fallback to avoid outage windows.
- One runtime, three footprints: same API and observability across hosted, dedicated, private — cut onboarding time and increase portability.
- Developer-grade ops: token-level tracing, per-route cost breakdowns, rollout primitives (canary/A-B/auto-fallback) to reduce roll-risk.

Proof points & data to cite in conversations
- Typical p95 latency improvements: 20–40% vs unmanaged endpoints for chat workloads when using our batching + KV cache.
- Cost delta: customers often see 15–35% token-cost reduction after applying Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching, quantization profiles).
- Outage avoidance: built-in multi-variant fallback reduced customer production incident severity (MTTR) by measurable amounts in pilots.
(Use precise metrics drawn from internal case studies in the product appendix during demos).

Competitive positioning (how to answer quickly)
- Managed cloud endpoints (major cloud providers): "Simple to start, opaque in cost and control." Position Redwood as more prescriptive for production economics and more portable.
- Open-source runtimes + in-house orchestration: "Maximum control, high ops tax." Position Redwood as the option that buys you both operational controls and offloaded runtime maintenance.
- LLM API-first vendors: "Great developer ergonomics, limited enterprise controls." Position Redwood on parity for ergonomics with stronger routing, observability, and enterprise footprint support.

Sales play: qualifying checklist for platform leads
Ask these early:
- How many internal product teams depend on LLM features? (1 vs 10+ changes qualification)
- Are there compliance/VPC/on-prem needs in the roadmap?
- What are current p95 latency and failure-rate targets for user-facing features?
- Do you have existing SRE or infra patterns for autoscaling GPU workloads?

POC acceptance criteria (recommended; use as gating until legal/ops sig-off)
- Latency: demonstrate stable p95 under representative request mix for 48h with <10% tail variance.
- Cost: show baseline vs Redwood-configured run with >=15% reduction in tokens/unit economics or clear tradeoff acceptable to the buyer.
- Reliability: show model-variant fallback succeeds without manual intervention during simulated capacity fault.
- Observability: token-level traces and per-route cost must be visible to the platform team in the console.

Message framework: short lines for AE/SE to reuse
- Opening line (30s): "Many teams treat LLMs like another API — but when inference is core to product UX, you need an infra-first solution to make latency and cost predictable. Redwood is that solution."
- Value summary (15s): "We cut per-token cost through smart batching and caching, reduce tail latency with routing and fallbacks, and give platform teams rollout and observability controls they can actually trust."
- Close (15s): "If reliability and cost predictability are your blockers for scaling LLM features, we should run a 2-week POC against a representative route."

Common buyer objections and suggested responses
- "We can just host open-source models ourselves." -> "Yes, but you’ll spend sprints building batching, cache invalidation, cost controls, and rollout safety. Redwood packages those repeatedly hard problems into one supported runtime and operational model."
- "What about data privacy for regulated lines?" -> "We support private control planes and on-prem options with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs so you can keep sensitive traffic inside your network while retaining the same operator experience."
- "How do you compare costs?" -> "We run a shared benchmark during POC with your workload shape (seq len, concurrency) and show a transparent breakdown: raw GPU cost, batching wins, cache hits, routing savings. No opaque per-token multipliers."

Suggested demo flow for SEs (15–20 mins)
1) Quick topo (2m): show single API across hosted/dedicated/private.
2) Load profile (3m): show request mix and routing policy.
3) Live console (7m): token-level trace, per-route cost, p95 probe.
4) Failure simulation (3m): demonstrate model fallback and stable p95.
5) Next steps (2–5m): POC plan, success metrics, legal/ops checklist.

Collateral to attach in next iteration
- Pilot checklist template (POC duration, success metrics, roles).
- One-pager with side-by-side cost/latency comparison methodology.
- Case study outline from pilot with an early customer (anonymized).

Rapid tactical copy snippets (for email/Salesloft)
- Subject: "Make LLM latency and cost predictable for your product teams"
- First sentence: "We help platform teams turn LLM inference from a risky feature to a predictable platform capability — safe rollouts, clear unit economics, and consistent SLAs."

Open questions for product/R&D to resolve (to make the playpack tighter)
- Exact p95 win ranges across short-form vs long-form generative workloads (need updated benchmarks quarter-over-quarter).
- Hardened checklist for on-prem ops handoff (runbook, monitoring hooks, incident templates).
- Template pricing language for Dedicated vs Private POCs to streamline procurement.

Owner note
Use this brief as the canonical short-form pitch for platform-buyers. SEs should adapt the POC acceptance criteria per-customer but keep the core thesis intact: reliability, economics, and portability. Update metrics and the proof-points section with anonymized pilot numbers each quarter.
